title: The Linux 7.4 Merge Window Is Easily The Largest In Kernel History
byline: Written by Michael Larabel in Linux Kernel on 1 November 2026 at 07:00 AM EST. 21 Comments
excerpt: After writing this morning with some stats about the size of the Linux 7.4 merge window and the kernel's source tree approaching 42 million lines, I was curious to run some numbers for putting the size of the merge window into perspective against the major kernel releases of the past 15 years
content_html:
After writing this morning with some stats about the size of the Linux 7.4 merge window and the kernel's source tree approaching 42 million lines, I was curious to run some numbers for putting the size of the merge window into perspective against the major kernel releases of the past 15 years. This shows the definite recent uptick due to AI/LLM activity.

The Linux kernel development pace has been on a definite upward trajectory over the past year. While, yes, Linux popularity is likely at an all-time high from consumer devices to massive growth in data centers, etc, a lot of the uptick in kernel patches is due to AI/LLMs. With Linux kernel maintainers being "completely overwhelmed" due to both AI generated bug reports and patches/fixes, the Git commit activity has been surging as a result.

For visualizing the impact, here is a look at the number of Git commits per Linux kernel merge window each release going back to Linux 3.1 -- released in 2011:

The Linux 7.4 merge window by far is the largest merge window ever in terms of commits/patches. Nearly 20k! The upward trend has continued building the past several kernel releases. Typically the merge windows saw 13~14k commits or less and now we are pushing 20k. Here's all the raw numbers for each merge window for those curious:

Granted, we could still see a few more trickle in today for Linux 7.4 ahead of the expected Linux 7.4-rc1 kernel release later in the day.

With much of the AI/LLM activity being around fixes, the surge in patches don't stop at the merge window. Here is a look at the number of Git commits for each kernel cycle in full from prior release to the tagged stable version:

Linux 7.3 was the first time breaching 20k commits for an entire kernel cycle (20,260 commits from v7.2 to v7.3). Now with Linux 7.4 we're seeing nearly that much just during the merge window.
